lead: A word like bank can mean a place that keeps money or the sloping ground beside a river. Word sense disambiguation (WSD) decides which listed sense a particular use carries. It needs a sense inventory such as WordNet, a context window around the target, and a decision rule: gloss overlap, a graph measure over the sense network, or a classifier trained on sense-tagged sentences. Machine translation, search and question answering all call WSD, because a wrong sense poisons everything downstream.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.3 for word senses and their relations, Chapter 4.4 for WordNet synsets and glosses, and Unit 5 for Naive Bayes if your course has covered it.

sections.h3: The task and the sense inventory

blocks.text: Word sense disambiguation (WSD) picks the sense a word carries in one particular use. The input is the target word, its sentence, and a sense inventory — a fixed list of the senses that word may have. The output is one label from that list.

The inventory fixes the granularity. Chapter 4.3 defines senses as distinct meanings of a word form; Chapter 4.4 shows WordNet storing each sense as a synset. Two systems are comparable only if they use the same inventory.
Lexical sample WSD disambiguates a few target words in many hand-tagged sentences. All-words WSD disambiguates every content word of a running text. Benchmark campaigns run both settings.

Context is the main evidence, taken from the words, their part-of-speech tags and their syntactic relations around the target. The context window is k words to each side of the target, with k usually between 5 and 10 in supervised systems; the whole sentence can be used when data are scarce. The word river near bank is strong evidence; the word the is none.

The most frequent sense baseline answers with the commonest sense of that word in a reference corpus. Senses are very unevenly distributed, so this baseline scores well above chance and every system must report it. WordNet lists senses roughly by frequency, so sense 1 is a ready-made guess.
The Lesk algorithm compares the dictionary gloss (definition) of each candidate sense with the words of the context, and picks the sense with the largest overlap.

blocks.where: s is one candidate sense of the target word; gloss(s) is the dictionary definition of s; context is the window text; |·| counts distinct content words.

items: Collect the content words of the context, dropping stop words and the target word.
Collect the content words of the gloss of each candidate sense.
Count the shared words for each sense and choose the largest count; break ties by a fixed rule.

blocks.text: Extended Lesk also uses glosses of senses related to each candidate — hypernyms, hyponyms, meronyms — so a short definition is backed by its neighbours. The gain in evidence brings extra noise.

Glosses hold six to ten words, so raw overlap is often zero and ties are common; a longer gloss then wins by accident. Two fixes: weight each shared word by how rare it is in a corpus, and normalise the score by gloss length.

Graph-based methods make nodes of the WordNet senses and edges of a similarity. Path length is one such similarity: fewer edges between two synsets means closer senses. The whole sentence is decoded at once — each sense starts with its gloss overlap and passes score to its neighbours until the values settle.
Supervised WSD trains a classifier on sentences whose target words are already sense-tagged. SemCor, a part of the Brown corpus tagged with WordNet senses, is a standard training source.

items: Words in a window of about ±5 to ±10, with stop words removed.
Part-of-speech tags of the neighbours; the tag of the target itself separates noun bank from verb bank.
Collocations and bigrams such as bank account or river bank.
Syntactic features from a dependency parse (Unit 3): head word, subject or object slot.

blocks.text: Naive Bayes needs little data but assumes features are independent given the sense. A decision tree gives readable rules. An SVM handles thousands of sparse features well. Unit 5 covers training.
Feature selection keeps features with high mutual information with the sense label and drops rare ones. Without it the feature vector is mostly zeros and training slows down.

sections.h3: Semi-supervised learning, evaluation and multilingual WSD

blocks.text: Bootstrapping starts from a few seed examples per sense, trains a classifier, labels unlabelled sentences, adds the most confident ones and repeats. Self-training uses one classifier. Co-training splits the features into two views — words left of the target and words right of it — and lets each classifier label data for the other.
One sense per discourse: a word usually keeps one sense through a document. Decoding the document jointly, choosing the assignment with the best total score, removes many isolated errors.
P = TP / (TP + FP)      R = TP / (TP + FN)      F1 = 2PR / (P + R)
blocks.where: TP is the items of a sense assigned correctly, FP items of other senses wrongly given that label, FN items of that sense given another label, P precision, R recall, F1 their harmonic mean.
correct items counts every test item whose predicted sense equals the gold sense.

blocks.text: Standard test sets come from the Senseval and SemEval campaigns, in lexical sample and all-words form. Report per-sense F1 and overall accuracy, and never tune on the test set. In cross-lingual WSD a parallel corpus supplies evidence: the translation chosen in another language narrows the sense, and multilingual wordnets give matching labels.

figure.caption: The context words around the target become a feature vector, a trained classifier scores each candidate sense, and the top sense is chosen. The decision rests on context, not on the word alone.

spec.title: Supervised WSD
spec.aria: A context window becomes a feature vector, a classifier scores the senses, and the highest-scoring sense is chosen.

examples.question: Disambiguate bank in 'The fisherman sat on the bank of the river.' (a) Run Lesk with glosses bank1 'a financial institution that accepts deposits' and bank2 'sloping land beside a river'. Count shared content words after removing stop words and the target. (b) Training counts are 30 finance and 10 river senses; the test set has 2 finance and 2 river items. What accuracy does the most frequent sense baseline reach?
steps: Remove stop words and the target. bank1 content: {financial, institution, accepts, deposits}. bank2 content: {sloping, land, beside, river}.
Overlap bank1 = 0 words; bank2 = {river} = 1 word. Lesk picks bank2, the river edge.
Training total = 40. Finance prior = 0.75; river prior = 0.25. The most frequent sense is finance.
The baseline labels all 4 test items finance: correct on 2 finance items, wrong on 2 river items.
examples.answer: Lesk returns the river sense with overlap 1 against 0, and the most frequent sense baseline scores 50 percent accuracy on the four-item test set.
examples.check:
gloss1 = {'financial','institution','accepts','deposits'}
gloss2 = {'sloping','land','beside','river'}
context = {'fisherman','sat','river'}
o1 = len(gloss1 & context)
o2 = len(gloss2 & context)
print(o1)
print(o2)
train_fin, train_riv = 30, 10
test_fin, test_riv = 2, 2
mfs = 'finance' if train_fin >= train_riv else 'river'
correct = test_fin if mfs == 'finance' else test_riv
acc = correct / (test_fin + test_riv)
print(acc)

traps: Skipping the most frequent sense baseline. A system that beats it by two points has done real work; without the baseline the number means nothing.
Tuning on the test set. Choosing k, the classifier or the tie rule by looking at test accuracy inflates the score; use a development split.
Letting gloss length decide. Lesk ties often go to the longer gloss, which had more chances to overlap. Normalise or weight the overlap.
Comparing accuracies across systems that used different sense inventories or granularity. The numbers are not on the same scale.
Stopping at the sentence. One sense per discourse means that another occurrence of the same word three sentences later can still correct the sense, so a document-level pass often helps.

quiz.q: Define word sense disambiguation and name its input and output.
quiz.a: WSD is the task of choosing the sense a target word carries in a given context. Input: target word, its sentence (context), and a sense inventory. Output: one sense label from that inventory.

quiz.q: Why is the most frequent sense baseline hard to beat?
quiz.a: Sense distributions are heavily skewed: a few senses cover most occurrences, so always answering with the commonest sense is right most of the time. The classifier must beat that bias, not chance.

quiz.q: Glosses for plant: plant1 'a living organism that grows in soil', plant2 'a factory that produces goods'. Context: 'The plant workers went on strike at the factory gate.' Compute the Lesk overlap for each sense and name the chosen sense. Stop words and the target are removed.
quiz.a: plant1 content {living, organism, grows, soil}; plant2 content {factory, produces, goods}; context content {workers, went, strike, factory, gate}. Overlap plant1 = 0, plant2 = {factory} = 1. Lesk chooses plant2, the factory sense.

quiz.q: Training data has 40 finance and 20 river examples of bank. The test set has 3 finance and 5 river items. What accuracy does the most frequent sense baseline get?
quiz.a: Finance prior = 40/60 = 0.67, river prior = 0.33, so the baseline always says finance. Correct = 3 of 8 items. Accuracy = 3/8 = 0.375, that is 37.5 percent.

quiz.q: Why does one sense per discourse help a WSD system, and how is it applied?
quiz.a: A word tends to keep one sense through a document, so local errors are correlated and can be removed by a global decision. Apply it by decoding the whole document jointly, for example with a chain over the occurrences, and picking the assignment with the best total score.

quiz.q: Extended Lesk raises overlap counts but can lower accuracy. Explain both effects.
quiz.a: Adding glosses of related senses increases the chance of a non-zero overlap, so fewer ties and more evidence. But those glosses belong to neighbouring senses, so words from a wrong sense's relatives can outvote the right one; without weighting, noise grows with the evidence.

quiz.q: What are the two views in co-training for WSD?
quiz.a: Two feature sets that are roughly independent, typically the words to the left of the target and the words to the right. Each classifier labels unlabelled data to enlarge the other's training set.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern WSD systems replace hand-built features with contextual embeddings, fine-tuning a pretrained encoder on sense-tagged data and then scoring each WordNet gloss. Sense inventories are being extended with automatically induced senses for domains and for languages with thin resources, and multilingual wordnets let one tagged corpus serve several languages. Unified evaluation frameworks that rerun every system on identical train and test splits are now the usual way to compare results. Search next for sense-annotated corpora, sense embeddings and WordNet gloss classification.
